detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Ioane led the Syrian mission in Georgia. By the mid-6th century he was already a well-known ascetic in Antioch, surrounded by twelve disciples. According to his vita, he decided to travel to Eastern Georgia after a vision of the Mother of God: in Kartli, then under Zoroastrian Persian rule, Christianity was already known, yet monasteries barely existed and the faith had a fragile hold. At the gates of Mtskheta, the newcomers were met by the ruler of Kartli and the head of the local church. Tradition is fond of that moment: Ioane and the Catholicos spoke different languages, yet supposedly understood each other right away without a translator.

Ioane did not stay at court and almost immediately climbed to the wooded ridge of Mount Zadeni across from Mtskheta. The site was not empty: long before Christianity, it had held a pagan sanctuary of Zaden, the Iberian deity of fertility. Setting up a Christian hermitage right over an old shrine was a gesture both practical and fairly blunt. At first all thirteen fathers lived here together in narrow hillside caves, but before long Ioane sent his disciples out across Kartli and Kakheti—not to stay tucked away in one monastery, but to head where Christian communities were weakest. Only one helper stayed behind with him.

Daily life on the mountain was rough: there was no water on the dry crest, while bears in the surrounding woods were plentiful. Medieval vitae say that after Ioane prayed, the animals stopped troubling pilgrims and walked calmly past his cell. The second problem was even more earthly—even a hermit cannot last on a waterless ridge. According to tradition, his prayer opened a cold spring right beside his cell. It still runs today, and locals believe its water helps with eye ailments.

Ioane spent the rest of his life on the mountain and asked to be buried in his own cell. When he died, his disciples first tried to carry him down to a more accessible monastery at the foot of the slope—but, as his vita tells it, an earthquake struck as soon as they brought the body off the ridge, forcing them to carry his relics back up. His tomb still lies in the northern aisle of the basilica, a few steps from that spring. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates Ioane as a Venerable Saint and the founder of Georgian monasticism.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: In the 8th century, the small 6th-century stone cell was rebuilt into a three-nave basilica. Builders did not tear down the older structure, but folded it neatly into the new church: the northern aisle incorporates the early 6th–7th-century chapel with Ioane's tomb and a rock-cut basin that still collects water from the spring. Inside, fragments of medieval frescoes and carved stone reliefs with early Georgian inscriptions survive.

Outside, remains of defensive walls, terraces, and later 17th-century fortifications wrap around the church. The ridge rises over a thousand meters, making it useful not just for solitude, but for watching the whole valley below: Mtskheta, Svetitskhoveli, Jvari on the neighboring hill, and the confluence of the Aragvi and Mtkvari rivers are all visible from here.

Today Zedazeni is an active men's monastery inside the Saguramo reserve. A narrow switchback road climbs up through beech and oak forest; the air at the top is almost always cooler than in Tbilisi or Mtskheta, and the stone terrace in front of the church is much quieter and less crowded than Jvari.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Of the fathers who headed into Kakheti, Stephane pushed farthest toward the eastern frontier of the kingdom. He settled on the slopes below present-day Signagi, beside the Khirsa stream. It was an unsettled borderland: raids regularly came down from the mountains and neighboring Caucasian Albania, while older pagan customs still held firm in surrounding villages. Rather than hiding in a remote cave, Stephane built an open monastery right among the frontier settlements.

He dedicated the monastery to St. Stephen the Protomartyr. According to local church tradition, the name was not chosen merely out of respect: a relic—the finger of Archdeacon Stephen—was kept near the altar. For a distant frontier outpost, that relic quickly made its mark: pilgrims began coming from across the area, turning the monastery into a steady anchor for local Christians.

Life on the border demanded resilience as well as preaching. Whenever raiders approached the villages, people retreated up the slopes, cut off from water in the lower valley. Tradition links a spring near the ravine beside the monastery to Stephane's prayers: water on higher ground sustained both monks and villagers whenever sieges blocked the valley below.

Stephane lived here to old age and was buried in the 6th-century basilica he founded. The church later burned, suffered earthquakes, and was rebuilt more than once, yet his raised stone tomb beside the northern wall near the altar was kept intact every time. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Stephane of Khirsa.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: Today's cathedral is a stack of several building periods. The 6th-century three-nave basilica was reworked into a domed church in the 10th century, then repaired heavily again in the 16th century after earthquakes and raids. Early Georgian Asomtavruli inscriptions from medieval rebuilds are still visible on the facade and near the apse.

A thick stone wall with remains of older fortifications encircles the church. In this corner of Kakheti, a monastery could not rely on prayer alone—heavy masonry offered shelter whenever trouble came. The old buildings sit on a gentle slope surrounded by trees and a quiet working courtyard.

Today Khirsa is an active men's monastery set among vineyards below Signagi, near the village of Tibaani. Because it sits slightly off the main tourist roads, the yard and Stephane's tomb are almost always quiet and uncrowded.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: While most of his companions headed into quiet mountains and gorges, Abibos took on a far more public and dangerous role as Bishop of Nekresi in Kakheti. In the 6th century, Sasanian Persian rule weighed heavily here: Zoroastrian fire temples stood next to Christian parishes, and Persian officials worked to weaken the local church. Abibos did not stay behind monastery walls—he traveled through the eastern mountain valleys, preached, baptized, and openly challenged Persian religious authority.

The best-known episode from his vita is short and blunt. One day Abibos walked straight into a Zoroastrian fire temple and poured water over the sacred altar, putting out the flame. In the eyes of Persian officials, that was no longer a theological dispute—it was a direct insult and a crime against the state.

Abibos was arrested, beaten, and marched under guard to face the Persian governor in Mtskheta. He never reached the trial: on the road, near the village of Rekha, he was stoned to death. Chronicles add that his body was left outside the walls for wild animals, which did not touch it. Christians buried him secretly at night, and later his relics were moved to Samtavro Cathedral in Mtskheta. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates Abibos as a Hieromartyr and patron of Kakheti.

Another local legend ties Nekresi to a later raid. When Muslim attackers approached the monastery, villagers supposedly slaughtered pigs and scattered the blood around the gates, after which the raiders chose not to enter. In memory of that story, Nekresi is still considered the only monastery in Georgia where pork is permitted at festive meals.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: Nekresi is not a single church, but a compact medieval ensemble on a wooded spur above the Alazani Valley. Its oldest building is older than Abibos himself: a tiny 4th-century basilica, one of the earliest stone churches in these lands. Around it later grew a 6th–7th-century three-church basilica and a 9th-century domed church with surviving fragments of medieval frescoes.

Beyond the churches, the ridge holds the ruins of a two-story bishop's palace, a watchtower, and a large stone marani—a wine cellar with clay qvevri sunk into the floor. Together they show how a hilltop monastery actually worked: it had to feed itself, store provisions, and hold out during a siege.

Today Nekresi is an active men's monastery. The road up the forested ridge is too steep for regular traffic, so visitors park at the bottom and ride a shuttle—or walk up the wooded slope—to the churches. From the upper terraces, wide views open over the Alazani plain and the vineyards below.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Tadeoz—affectionately called Tate in Georgia—was in no rush to leave his teacher. When the other fathers dispersed across Kartli and Kakheti, he stayed at the foot of Mount Zedazeni to care for the aging Ioane and founded a small monastery dedicated to St. Stephen the Protomartyr. That place, Stepantsminda, gave him his epithet Stepantsmindeli. It has nothing to do with the northern mountain town of Kazbegi, now also called Stepantsminda, though the two are confused constantly.

Only after receiving Ioane's blessing did Tadeoz head west into Shida Kartli. He walked through villages around Urbnisi and Kaspi, preaching and strengthening small Christian communities where older pagan habits still lingered. He worked quietly and without hurry, staying in local parishes for long stretches.

In time Tadeoz left the valley villages for Mount Tslevi above Kaspi, settling in the wooded limestone gorge of Tetrakhevi, meaning "White Gorge." According to his vita, he carved a small cell into the rock and lived there in silence and prayer. As often happened with hermits, solitude did not last long: shepherds and peasants from nearby villages kept climbing the gorge for advice, blessings, and healing.

Tadeoz lived to old age and, according to tradition, was buried here at Tetrakhevi—though the exact spot of his grave has never been established. Even though his name is less widely known than Davit's or Shio's, local memory of him never faded. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Tadeoz of Stepantsminda.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: Tetrakhevi Monastery sits on the slopes of Mount Tslevi near Kaspi, among pale limestone outcrops and brushwood. The late medieval hall church was built of rough-hewn local stone on the site of the earlier monastery, while older cave cells survive in the surrounding rocky slopes, most of them now hard to reach.

Unlike the other sites on this map, Tetrakhevi survives only in ruins: the vault and parts of the walls have collapsed, the roof is gone, and only roofless stone walls remain standing in the gorge. In the 2000s, local residents cleared away rubble and uncovered traces of an old monastic ossuary, though full restoration has never taken place.

Today it is an inactive monastery and one of the quietest, least visited of all thirteen sites. There is no paved road here: visitors reach the ruins on foot or by off-road vehicle along the dirt tracks above Kaspi.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Zenon did not go looking for deserts or sheer cliffs: he settled in a gentle valley at the foot of the Gombori range, not far from Telavi. His goal was not extreme austerity, but a steady monastic community able to teach, copy books, and run its own estate.

That practical choice paid off many times over. Centuries later, in the early 12th century, King David the Builder invited the renowned philosopher and theologian Arsen Ikaltoeli here to turn the monastery into a higher school. Ikhalto became one of the chief centers of learning in medieval Georgia.

At the Ikhalto Academy, students studied theology, astronomy, mathematics, rhetoric, metalworking, and medicine—and judging by the massive stone wine presses in the yard, winemaking received just as much attention. Georgian tradition counts the poet Shota Rustaveli among the academy's students, though no direct written proof survives.

Zenon himself spent his whole life here and was buried in the Church of the Transfiguration (Khvtaeba), beneath the southern vault near the altar. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Zenon of Ikhalto; his individual feast day is 30 October.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: Within Ikhalto's compact yard, buildings from different centuries stand side by side. The oldest is the modest 6th-century domed Church of the Holy Spirit (Sameba), which preserves Zenon's own cell on its second level. Next to it rises the 8th–9th-century Church of the Transfiguration, built over the earlier basilica holding his grave.

A short step away stand the ruins of the 12th-century Academy: stone walls with tall arched windows, a spacious lecture hall, scriptorium niches, a stone grape press (satsnakheli), and buried clay qvevri. The building's roof was burned in 1616 by the army of Shah Abbas I during his devastating campaign in Kakheti.

Today Ikhalto is an active church complex and an open historical monument shaded by tall old cypress trees. Visitors can wander freely through the roofless academy walls and former wine cellars, and in summer it stays noticeably cooler here than down in the valley.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Davit began right within the bounds of present-day Tbilisi, living in a cave on the slope of Mount Mtatsminda—the hill's name ("Holy Mountain") is linked to him. Every week he walked down into the town to preach, yet the noise and attention weighed on him. With his disciple Lukiane he moved south into the treeless Gareja semi-desert on the modern border between Georgia and Azerbaijan. The land was dry and harsh, so both cells and water cisterns had to be cut straight into the sandstone.

Medieval vitae preserve two especially well-known stories about Davit. In the first, the hermits in the steppe survived in their early years on the milk of wild deer that came to their cave on their own. When a serpent living in the rocks swallowed a fawn, Davit struck it with his staff and lightning destroyed the creature—a scene frequently painted on Georgian frescoes.

The second legend tells of Davit's pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Walking all the way to a hill outside the city walls, he judged himself unworthy to step inside the holy city, prayed from afar, and picked up three stones from the ground as a keepsake. That night an angel warned the Patriarch of Jerusalem that the monk was carrying away "all the grace of Jerusalem." Messengers caught up with Davit on the road and took back two stones, leaving him one—the so-called "Stone of Grace."

Over time, hundreds of monks gathered around Davit's cave, turning the empty steppe into a major monastic center. Davit was buried in the cave Church of the Transfiguration at the Lavra, where the Stone of Grace was also kept before being moved to Sioni Cathedral in Tbilisi. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Davit of Gareja, celebrating Davitgarejoba on the Thursday after Ascension.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: The David Gareja Lavra is carved straight into a layered sandstone cliff. Around Davit's original 6th-century cleft, monks from the 9th to the 13th century excavated hundreds of cells, refectories with stone benches, bakeries, and chapels, gradually turning the surrounding hills into a whole network of desert monasteries.

In a waterless semi-desert, survival depended on ingenuity and engineering as much as fasting: monks cut a web of narrow gutters into the tilted rock strata to catch rare rainwater and channel it into deep underground cisterns.

Today the lower Lavra is an active men's monastery at the end of a long drive across open steppe. Some chapels on the upper ridge, including Udabno with its famous frescoes, lie along a disputed stretch of the border with Azerbaijan, so it is best to check access conditions before visiting.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: After parting with Ioane of Zedazeni, Ioseb moved into northern Kakheti, onto the wide plain of the Alazani River at the foot of the Greater Caucasus. According to tradition, the area was sparsely settled then, and neighboring highlanders came down here for seasonal festivals of a moon deity. Ioseb built a small church dedicated to St. George; his vita mentions that he wore a cross containing a fragment of the True Cross.

Medieval hagiography links the monastery's later rise to a chance encounter on a hunt. A local nobleman riding through the thickets of the Alazani plain came across the lone monk at prayer. Impressed by the encounter and the relic Ioseb carried, he paid for the first stone church and enlisted neighboring villages to protect the small community.

From that modest 6th-century church grew one of the main spiritual centers of Eastern Georgia. Five centuries later, in the early 11th century, Kakhetian rulers raised a vast cathedral on the same spot—a church that remained the tallest in Georgia for nearly a thousand years.

Ioseb was buried in the church he founded, and when the 11th-century cathedral was built, his tomb was carefully preserved in the northern part of the sanctuary. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Ioseb of Alaverdi. Every late September, people from across Kakheti and the mountain gorges still gather here for the traditional festival of Alaverdoba.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: In the early 11th century, St. George Cathedral was raised directly over the foundations of the 6th-century church. Standing more than fifty meters tall, it can be spotted across the flat plain from far away; a fortified stone wall encloses the grounds, while the austere facades are articulated with restrained blind arcades.

Inside, the cathedral feels unusually tall and spacious. Once 19th-century whitewash was cleaned off the walls, medieval frescoes of the 11th, 15th, and 16th centuries came back into view—among them the Virgin and Child in the apse and a rare portrait of Ioseb directly above his tomb.

Today Alaverdi is an active men's monastery and the seat of the local metropolitan. The monks run a large working estate: they tend vineyards and beehives, and still ferment wine in an ancient stone marani dating from the 8th–11th centuries.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Anton's epithet tells you nearly everything about his character: Martqopi comes from Georgian marto-mkopi, "the one who lives alone." Together with the other Syrian fathers, he brought a famed relic to these lands—a ceramic tile bearing the Image of Christ Not Made by Hands, linked by tradition to the ancient image from Edessa in Syria. For his home, Anton chose the dense wooded hills east of present-day Tbilisi.

For a while no one knew he was there, until a royal hunting party stumbled upon his tame deer in the forest. Word of the hermit spread quickly, and villagers from nearby settlements soon began coming up for advice and healing. His quiet hideout gradually turned into a busy monastery.

To keep his vow of silence without turning people away, Anton found a simple yet radical answer—he went upward. On a rocky ridge above the monastery he built a narrow stone tower and spent the last fifteen years of his life on its top as a stylite, counseling disciples from above and pulling food up in a basket on a rope.

After his death, his disciples brought his body down from the pillar and buried him in the main monastery church, by the north wall before the icon of the Mother of God. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Anton of Martqopi; his feast day is 29 August, the feast of the Image Not Made by Hands.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: The monastery occupies two levels: the main courtyard in the wooded hollow below, and Anton's pillar high on the ridge above. The 6th-century church where the Edessa relic was kept suffered heavily during invasions—above all Timur's campaign of 1395, when monks hid the icon and later moved it to Tbilisi; it is now kept in the Georgian National Museum.

Most buildings in the lower courtyard date to the 17th–19th centuries, including a tall mid-19th-century bell tower. From the monastery wall, a steep forest trail takes about twenty minutes up to a reconstructed stone tower standing on the foundations of Anton's original pillar.

Today Martqopi is an active men's monastery tucked into dense forest not far from Tbilisi. The city is close by, yet behind the hills and trees the place feels completely quiet, and the short climb to the tower is a natural part of the visit.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Unlike the companions who withdrew to caves and deep forests, Ise was given administrative and pastoral work. According to tradition, Ioane of Zedazeni and the head of the local church ordained him Bishop of Tsilkani and put him in charge of a major cathedral on the Mukhrani plain northwest of Mtskheta.

His diocese stretched north into the mountain valleys at the foot of the Caucasus range, where Christian parishes were still sparse. Ise traveled from village to village, preaching, organizing church life, and dealing directly with the everyday concerns of farming communities.

The best-known tradition about Ise involves a very earthly trouble—drought. When the fields around Tsilkani began drying out while the Ksani River flowed at a distance, his vita recounts that Ise walked down to the bank, touched the water with his bishop's staff, and told it to follow him. Walking back and drawing a line in the earth with his staff, he supposedly led a stream all the way to Tsilkani, starting the village's irrigation canal.

Ise served his see into old age and was buried in the Tsilkani Cathedral of the Mother of God, beneath the floor between the sanctuary and the northern choir. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Ise, Bishop and Wonderworker of Tsilkani; his feast day is 15 December.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: The church at Tsilkani is older than Ise himself: it was founded in the 4th–5th century, soon after Kartli adopted Christianity. In the 5th–6th centuries it was reworked into a three-nave basilica and later rebuilt as a domed cathedral.

In the 18th century, a sturdy stone wall with round corner towers was raised around the church—during raids, both clergy and villagers took shelter behind it. Inside, early medieval carved stone reliefs and a venerated copy of the 9th-century Tsilkani Icon of the Mother of God survive.

Today Tsilkani is an active cathedral and village parish church about twenty minutes' drive from Mtskheta. A stone slab inside marks Bishop Ise's grave, and behind the defensive wall the yard has a calm, unhurried village atmosphere.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Shio, called the Cave-Dweller, went west from Mtskheta along the northern bank of the Mtkvari and settled in a narrow limestone gorge, inside a shallow cleft in the cliff. His search for quiet produced a familiar hermit's paradox: word of him spread quickly across Kartli, and chronicles claim up to two thousand monks eventually gathered in the canyon, forming one of the largest monastic communities in medieval Georgia.

Medieval vitae preserve plenty of vivid details from his early years in the gorge. They say a dove brought the hermit food at first, and when the growing brotherhood could not agree on where to build the first church, Shio burned incense right on his bare palm without injury and told them to build wherever the smoke settled.

Later, tired of renown and constant visits from the nobility, Shio carried the idea of seclusion to its limit. He had a vertical pit—mgvime in Georgian—about ten meters deep dug straight into the limestone. Tradition says he spent his last fifteen years at the bottom, receiving bread and water lowered in a basket through a narrow opening above.

He was buried at the bottom of that same pit, which became a crypt for his relics. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Shio the Cave-Dweller (Shio Mgvimeli); his feast is observed on Cheesefare Thursday, right before Great Lent.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: Because the monastery grew around a vertical cave in a tight canyon, its buildings rise in tiers right along the cliff. The oldest is the 6th-century octagonal domed Church of St. John the Baptist, set partly into the rock beside the mouth of Shio's pit.

Higher up stands the 11th–12th-century Upper Church (Zemo Eklesia), founded under David the Builder and later rebuilt in brick and stone after Persian and Mongol raids. Behind the churches, more than a hundred cave cells from the 6th–12th centuries are cut into the pale limestone wall.

Today Shio-Mgvime is an active men's monastery a few kilometers west of Mtskheta. Inside the 6th-century church you can see the opening of the deep pit where Shio lived for fifteen years, while the tall canyon walls keep the courtyard shaded and cool for much of the day.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Isidore—called Ezderios in early chronicles—traveled west from Mtskheta into the fertile valley of Shida Kartli and stopped on the left bank of the Lekhura River. He did not withdraw into remote mountains: right among the farming villages, he founded the Church of the Ascension and a missionary school.

Instead of an isolated hermitage, Samtavisi became a lively center of teaching, preaching, and relief for surrounding villages. Over time it grew into an important episcopal seat anchoring church life in this part of Kartli.

The site's greatest artistic fame arrived five hundred years later. In 1030, a local bishop and master builder raised a new cross-domed cathedral over Isidore's grave. The carving on its eastern facade—a tall ornamental cross flanked by diamond rosettes, with a griffin beneath the window—proved so compelling that Georgian builders repeated variations of it on new churches for roughly the next two centuries.
Isidore's tomb lies inside Samtavisi Cathedral, on the northern side of the sanctuary. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Isidore (Ezderios) of Samtavisi.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: Nothing of Isidore's original 6th-century basilica remains above ground, yet the 1030 cathedral survives in remarkably good shape—even though a 15th-century earthquake brought down its original dome and western wall. That carved eastern facade remains one of the most recognizable landmarks of medieval Georgian architecture.

Inside the apse, 17th-century frescoes survive, and a stone canopy marks Isidore's grave. Next to the cathedral stand a fortified bishop's residence and a two-story 17th-century bell tower built directly into the defensive wall.

Today Samtavisi is an active cathedral and episcopal residence just a few minutes off the main highway near Kaspi. It is easier to reach than almost any other of the thirteen sites, yet the spacious walled yard usually stays peaceful.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Piros settled on the bank of the Dvani River at Breti, near present-day Kareli in Shida Kartli. Medieval church hymns call him a "divine image of repentance" for his strict fasting and long night vigils, yet he never cut himself off from ordinary people.

His monastery served as a refuge for the poor, the sick, and those with nowhere else to turn. No dramatic mountain miracle tales grew up around Piros's name—instead, memory preserved a quiet, steady ascetic and a monastery woven into the life of nearby villages.

Curiously, the best-known historical work linked to Breti is neither a cave nor a fortress wall, but a piece of goldsmithing. In the 11th century, a medieval master made a processional cross for the monastery: a wooden core sheathed in chased silver and gold plates with scenes from the life of Christ and Georgian inscriptions. It survived centuries of raids and is now kept in the Georgian National Museum in Tbilisi.

Piros was buried in the small 6th-century church he built at Breti. When the monastery was later expanded, builders left his original chapel standing as the northern burial chamber. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Piros of Breti; his feast day is 28 May.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: Breti shows clearly how medieval builders treated earlier shrines: directly against the southern wall of Piros's modest 6th-century hall church, they added the larger 8th–9th-century St. George hall church of yellowish sandstone, leaving the older chapel intact.

During restoration, removing layers of soot and later whitewash revealed fragments of 11th–13th-century frescoes depicting the Church Fathers, alongside medieval Georgian graffiti scratched into the plaster by pilgrims over the centuries.
Today Breti is a quiet village church and small monastic complex surrounded by orchards in the Kareli district. A low stone doorway leads straight from the main church into Piros's burial chamber.

detailSections.heading: The Saint
paragraphs: Mikhail went farthest west of all the fathers. He crossed the Likhi range dividing Eastern and Western Georgia and settled in the wooded gorge of the Cheratkhevi River near Surami, on a mountain slope beside the old roads linking the two Georgian kingdoms. There he founded Ulumbo Monastery.

Very few early written accounts of Mikhail survive, and for a concrete reason: around 1400, Timur's army sacked Ulumbo and burned its library and archives. Whatever the monks had recorded about their founder perished in the fire.

Memory of the saint rested instead on local oral tradition—stories about a spring he blessed in the gorge, and about the Ulumbo Icon of the Mother of God. Villagers are said to have carried the icon deep into the woods whenever foreign armies crossed the pass.

Twentieth-century excavations uncovered a tomb directly in front of the altar of the Ulumbo church, matching the long-standing belief that Mikhail was buried in the chancel of his church. The Georgian Orthodox Church venerates him as Venerable Mikhail of Ulumbo; his feast is observed on the third day after Ascension.

detailSections.heading: The Monastery
paragraphs: The Church of the Assumption of the Mother of God at Ulumbo stands in the woods above the village of Alisiubani. Both the 6th-century church and its medieval successors were destroyed repeatedly during Timur's invasion and later Ottoman raids.

Local noble families rebuilt the church in the 17th–18th centuries and again in 1871. Surviving carved reliefs and cornice stones from the ruined medieval churches were not discarded, but neatly set into the exterior masonry of the new walls, where they are easy to spot as you walk around.

Today Ulumbo is an active monastery tucked into the forest of the Khashuri district. A dirt road leads up to it alongside a mountain stream, keeping highway noise far away and the woods around it calm.
